events.text: A drummer walks through your village beating the call for {hw_side}. Behind him the miller's boys fall in, then the cooper, then a goat that nobody claims. The drummer stops at your door and keeps drumming until you open it.

effects.log: You fall in behind the goat. By the next village there are forty of you, and the drummer has started a song.
The drumming goes on outside for a while, offended, and then moves on.
He drinks, thanks you and tells you the truth about the war: it is about a toll bridge.

events.text: Your old fighting school has declared for {hw_side} in the Feud of the Schools. The master, a bent old woman called Granny Ahn, sends a boy with one word written on a board: 'Well?'

effects.log: Granny Ahn looks you up and down and hands you a staff. 'Still slow on the left,' she says. You are in.

choices.text: Write 'No' on the back of the board.

effects.log: The boy carries it back. Granny Ahn, they say, laughed and hung it on the wall.

events.text: A priest of the maker-god nobody has seen preaches in the square that {hw_side} has the maker's blessing. A priest of the same temple, two streets away, says the same of {hw_foe}. You stand between them and feel, oddly, that neither is right.

choices.text: Ask them both what the maker wants.

effects.log: Both answer at once. Neither answer fits. You walk home with a strange certainty you cannot explain.
You enlist. The first priest blesses you. The second blesses you too, to be safe.

events.text: The recruiter for {hw_side} offers to pay off your family's debt to the grain lender if you sign. The debt is old and heavy. The war is new and heavier.

effects.log: The grain lender tears up the note in front of you. The neighbours cry. You march in the morning.
You work the debt off over years. It is slower, and nobody dies of it.

events.text: Your oldest friend, Gyeol the blacksmith's son, has already joined {hw_foe}, because his mother's kin live over the hills. He comes by at night to say goodbye and to ask you not to join the other side.

effects.log: You promise. He leaves easier. The village calls you a coward for a season.
You tell him you will try not to meet him. He laughs and says that is how these things always go.

events.text: The armies meet at a ford on {hw_field}. The river is low and very cold. Whoever holds the far bank holds the road to {pw_kingdom}'s capital.

ok.log: You cross under a rain of stones and hold the bank until the rest arrive.

fail.log: The current takes your feet. You are dragged out downstream, half drowned.

effects.log: You wade the ford a dozen times with men and women on your back. The water is very cold.

events.text: In the Feud of the Schools, the fight in the market is staves against staves. Your opponent is a student of {hw_foe} no older than you, with a nose that has clearly been broken before.

ok.log: You knock the staff from his hands. He bows, picks it up and runs.

fail.log: He breaks your nose this time. Now you match.

choices.text: Knock over the fruit stall between you.

effects.log: The stall-keeper chases you both out of the market with a broom. The feud is postponed.

events.text: {hw_cmdr} has put the archers of {hw_foe} on a hill above the road. Your company has to pass beneath it. Your captain says to run.

effects.log: You run. Arrows fall behind you. You make the far woods with your breath in rags.

choices.text: Go up the back of the hill.

ok.log: You find a goat path and come up behind the archers. They surrender to five muddy soldiers.

fail.log: The goat path ends in a cliff. You climb back down and run with the others, late.

events.text: In the charge your horse is struck and goes down. It is a farm horse called Barley, borrowed from a neighbour, and it is still alive, screaming in the mud.

effects.log: You stay with Barley until the fight passes. The horse lives, lame. Your neighbour forgives you.
You fight on foot. When you go back, Barley is gone, taken by someone, alive.

events.text: The fighting has reached a village. The villagers are hiding in the temple of the maker-god. {hw_Foe} wants the temple as a strongpoint. So does your captain.

choices.text: Keep the fight away from the temple.

effects.log: You lead your squad round the long way. The temple stands. The villagers come out after.
You take it. The villagers are moved to the cellars. Nobody is hurt. Nobody thanks you.

events.text: The two schools agree to settle a quarrel by a single bout, as the old custom is. {hw_Side} chooses you. {hw_cmdr} sends a champion with very long arms.

ok.log: You win the bout. The quarrel is settled for a year. The champion buys you tea.

fail.log: The long arms win. You are carried off to cheers and boos in equal measure.

choices.text: Ask for a different contest: a race.

effects.log: Both schools are so surprised they agree. You win by a nose and nobody quite knows what it settled.

events.text: It rains so hard on {hw_field} that both armies stop. Bowstrings are wet, the ground is soup and nobody can see the banners.

effects.log: You sing an old harvest song. After a while someone on the other side sings the second verse.
You move your squad round the flank in the rain. When it clears, you are on their side of the field.

events.text: The toll bridge the war is about stands between the armies. {hw_Foe} plans to burn it. The bridge-keeper, an old man called Wol, refuses to leave it.

ok.log: Wol comes, grumbling, carrying his toll box. The bridge burns. Wol does not forgive anyone.

fail.log: Wol will not move. The bridge does not burn, because nobody will burn it with Wol on it.

effects.log: You hold the bridge with an old man and his toll box. It is the strangest fight of the war, and you win it.

events.text: The camp cook, a huge gentle man called Big Dol, has made the same bean soup for forty days. The soldiers have started writing poems about it, none of them kind.

effects.log: Your poem is read out at supper. Big Dol cries and puts an onion in tomorrow.
You forage for garlic. The soup improves overnight. Big Dol tells everyone it was his idea.

events.text: A soldier in your tent, Suni, asks you to read her a letter from home. Her little brother has learned to write, and the letter is in his giant crooked hand.

effects.log: It is about a frog. Suni laughs until she cries. So does the whole tent.

choices.text: Teach her to read it herself.

effects.log: It takes the rest of the campaign. She reads his next letter alone.

events.text: Half the company's boots have rotted in the wet. The quartermaster says new boots are coming. The quartermaster has said that before.

effects.log: You teach the company to plait straw sandals, as the old people of your village did. They march, laughing at their feet.

choices.text: March to the next town and demand boots.

effects.log: The town's cobbler gives you twenty pairs on credit. The quartermaster never pays him.

events.text: At night a soldier of your company, a farmer called Pil, tells you his fields will rot if he is not home for the harvest, and his children will go hungry.

effects.log: Pil goes home. You stand his watches for a month and say he is ill.
The captain grants him harvest leave, to everyone's surprise. Pil comes back with a sack of apples for the company.

events.text: A thin yellow dog follows the army. The soldiers feed it scraps. It barks at night when anyone approaches, and has twice woken the camp for a raid.

effects.log: You call it Sentry. The whole camp calls it Sentry. It sleeps across your feet.
You make a collar of red cloth. The captain enters it on the roll as a soldier, as a joke, and pays it a ration.

events.text: A pedlar in the camp sells needles and asks too many questions about the captain's tent.

ok.log: She meets a scout of {hw_foe} at the stream. You bring the captain to watch.

fail.log: You lose her in the reeds.

choices.text: Tell her the captain sleeps in the latrine.

effects.log: She writes it down. You wonder what {hw_foe} makes of it.

events.text: Granny Ahn, the old master of your school, has followed the army in a cart, because, she says, the young ones still drop their guard on the left.

effects.log: She makes you practise until your arms ache. You are faster in the next fight.

choices.text: Ask her about the last feud.

effects.log: She tells you about a feud sixty years ago and the boy she fought in it, whom she later married.

events.text: A fever goes through the camp. The army healer is a young man who learned medicine from a book and is learning very fast.

ok.log: You boil water and keep the sick apart. The fever passes with few lost.

fail.log: You catch it yourself and spend a week sweating in a tent.

effects.log: She comes, scolds the healer and saves the camp with willow bark.

events.text: As {hw_rank} you command a company of farmers, apprentices and one disgraced noble's son who keeps saying he should be in charge.

effects.log: He is terrible at it, and learns that in public. He is a better soldier after.
He carries the pots and sulks. The company loves you.

events.text: The general orders your company to burn the barns of the villages ahead, so {hw_foe} will find no food. The villagers are {pw_kingdom}'s own people.

effects.log: You burn the barns. {hw_Foe} goes hungry. So do the villagers.

choices.text: Empty the barns and carry the grain.

effects.log: You carry off the grain for the army and leave the barns. The villagers will rebuild faster.
You refuse. The general relieves you for a month. The villagers hear of it.

events.text: Your best scout, a quiet girl called Nabi, says {hw_cmdr}'s army is not where the general thinks. The general does not believe scouts who are girls.

choices.text: Take her report to the general yourself.

effects.log: The general believes you, and acts. Nabi is not thanked. You make sure she is paid double.

choices.text: Act on it without telling him.

effects.log: You move your company. When {hw_foe} attacks, you are there. The general claims he planned it.

events.text: After the battle at {hw_field} you must write to the families of eleven of your soldiers. You knew all of them. One of them owed you a coin.

effects.log: It takes all night. One family writes back to thank you.

choices.text: Visit the nearest families in person.

effects.log: You walk to three villages. It is the hardest march of the war.

events.text: Your company has taken prisoners from {hw_foe}: a dozen apprentices of a rival school, frightened and hungry.

choices.text: Feed them and let them go.

effects.log: They go home and tell their school who fed them. Next time you meet them, they fight less hard.
They are sent to the rear and fed thin. The general is pleased.

events.text: It was you who called the feud. In the market people stop talking when you pass. A boy throws a stone at your back and runs off. His father was hurt at {hw_field}.

effects.log: You sit with the father. He says nothing kind, and lets you stay.
You keep walking. The stone stays in your mind more than the bruise.

events.text: The village council asks you, the one who began the war, how long it will last. They have to know how much grain to keep.

effects.log: They keep grain for a year. You find out what a year means.
They are angry at the truth and keep grain for three. It is the right amount.

events.text: {hw_cmdr} sends a message: end the war you began, and keep the toll bridge, but give back the hill. Your captains say you could have both.

effects.log: The war ends with an argument nobody wins. Many go home who would not have.
You fight for the hill. You get the hill. It costs more than the bridge ever earned.

events.text: An old woman of your village, who never asked anything of you, walks into your tent and asks you to end it.

effects.log: She nods and goes home. Your letters to her are the only honest ones you write all war.
She looks at you for a long time and goes home. She sends you a scarf.

events.text: {hw_Side} is in retreat. The road is full of carts, cows, children and wounded. {hw_Foe}'s riders are an hour behind.

ok.log: You hold it with twenty soldiers and a cart until the road is empty.

fail.log: You hold it half the time you hoped. Most of the road gets through.

effects.log: You load children into carts until there are no more carts. Then you carry the last two.

events.text: Your company is hungry. A farmhouse nearby has bread cooling on the sill. The farmer is old and alone.

choices.text: Buy it with your last coins.

effects.log: The farmer takes the coins and gives you twice the bread.
You take it. The company eats. The farmer watches from the door.

events.text: The hall of your fighting school has been taken by {hw_foe}. Granny Ahn's training posts are being used for firewood.

effects.log: You creep in at night and carry out the school's tablet of names. Granny Ahn does not speak for a day, and then hugs you.
A school is its people, Granny Ahn says, and the people are alive. She says it twice, to convince herself.

events.text: A captain of {hw_foe} offers you a place on their side. Your side is losing. The pay is better. The captain is not unkind.

effects.log: You refuse. The captain nods, as if it was what he expected.

choices.text: Ask for terms for your company instead.

effects.log: He gives terms: your company may go home unharmed. Many do.

events.text: {hw_Side} takes a market town of {hw_foe}. The soldiers want to loot it. The townsfolk have barricaded their doors.

effects.log: You post guards. The town is spared, and opens its doors to sell you bread.
You take a fine pair of boots. They fit very well and feel very heavy.

events.text: The general holds a feast for the victory. He seats you beside him and asks your opinion of the next campaign. Everyone is listening.

choices.text: Say it is time to stop.

effects.log: The table goes quiet. The general laughs too loudly. A month later, he stops.

choices.text: Say what he wants to hear.

effects.log: He beams. You are seated beside him at every feast now.

events.text: {hw_cmdr} has been captured. The general wants to hang his banner upside down over the gate. {hw_cmdr} asks only to send a letter to his daughter.

effects.log: You carry it. His daughter sends back a sprig of plum blossom for him.

choices.text: Let the general have his way.

effects.log: The banner hangs upside down. {hw_Foe} will remember it for a generation.

events.text: The toll bridge the war was about is now in your side's hands. The general proposes doubling the toll. The farmers who use it are your own people.

effects.log: The general says no. The farmers hear you argued. It matters to them.
The toll doubles. The bridge is busy, and resented.

events.text: The harvest is ripe and the young have gone to the war. In the fields of your village there are only grandparents and small children with sickles too big for them.

effects.log: You work from dawn to dark. The granary is full by the first frost.
You turn the harvest into a contest with prizes of honey cake. The children win everything.

events.text: The list of the dead from {hw_field} is nailed to the temple door. A crowd reads it in silence. An old woman beside you cannot read.

effects.log: You read every name. Her grandson's is not there. She holds your hand very hard.

choices.text: Stay until everyone has read it.

effects.log: You stay all day and read the list to anyone who asks.

events.text: Refugees from the border villages have come to your village with their cows and their grief. The headman says there is no room.

effects.log: You fill your barn with two families and a cow. The headman is ashamed and finds more room.
You fix the roof of the old mill. By spring it is a village of its own.

events.text: The grain merchant has raised his prices because of the war. The village bakery has had to close.

ok.log: The crowd jeers. He lowers his prices.

fail.log: He jeers back. The crowd laughs at both of you.

choices.text: Buy flour from the next valley.

effects.log: You walk the flour back on your back. The bakery opens for one more month.

events.text: A widow of the war runs the inn now. She does not talk about her husband. His staff stands by the door.

effects.log: You mend the roof. She feeds you for a week and says nothing about it.
She tells you, over one cup, everything about him. Then she does not talk about him again.

events.text: The village children play the war: {hw_side} against {hw_foe}. Nobody wants to be {hw_foe}, so the smallest child always is, and always loses.

effects.log: You lose loudly and dramatically. The smallest child wins, once.

choices.text: Teach them a game about building a bridge.

effects.log: They build a mud bridge across the ditch and fight over the toll.

events.text: The temple's priest asks you to pray to the maker-god for the war to end. When you kneel at the altar, you feel the oddest thing: as if the prayer is coming in, not going out.

effects.log: You pray. Nothing answers, except a deep, unaccountable sadness for the whole world.
You stand up and the feeling goes. The priest looks at you strangely.

events.text: The toll bridge burned in the war is being rebuilt. The carpenter in charge is the soldier of {hw_foe} who set it on fire. He was ordered to. He has volunteered to rebuild it.

effects.log: You work a season beside him. When it is done, he carves both your names on the rail.
You bring lunch every day. The village is outraged, then curious, then brings lunch too.

events.text: The two schools of the old feud hold a joint festival of forms. The masters glare at each other, the students show off and everyone eats.

effects.log: You perform badly and with great enthusiasm. Both masters applaud, to spite each other.
You judge fairly. Both schools complain. That is how you know you were fair.

events.text: An old soldier of the last war sits by the well each morning, his leg stiff. The children tease him. He tells them stories, which are better than they expected.

effects.log: You hear about a night march you were on yourself. His version has more owls in it.
You make him a chair with a back. He sits in it like a king.

events.text: Two families in your village are still feuding about who betrayed whom in the war. Nobody remembers what happened. Everybody remembers who to hate.

ok.log: You find that nobody betrayed anybody. A bridge collapsed. Both families are furious to lose the grudge.

fail.log: You find nothing, and both families suspect you now.

effects.log: You introduce the eldest son of one to the eldest daughter of the other. It takes three years. The feud ends at a wedding.

events.text: {pw_kingdom}'s council wants a stone for the fallen of the last war. Each village wants its own names first.

choices.text: Suggest the names in the order they fell.

effects.log: It is slow and fair. Nobody is happy. Everyone visits.

choices.text: Suggest a tree for each village.

effects.log: They plant a row of trees on the hill. In a century it is a wood.

events.text: A pedlar brings word that a lord in the next valley is buying spears. Nobody else seems worried.

effects.log: The council thanks you and does nothing. In ten years they are very sorry.

ok.log: You find the spears are for a hunt of wild boar. You eat boar.

fail.log: You find the spears and the lord's son, who wants a war. You tell everyone.

events.text: The village school needs a teacher. The last one went to the war and did not come back. The children are running wild.

effects.log: You teach letters, sums and the names of the stars. One child becomes a scholar.
You find a retired clerk who drinks. He is a very good teacher when sober, which is mornings.

events.text: You call on the hall of the school across the hills, under a white cloth. Their master, a long-faced man called Teacher Ryeo, serves you tea and watches your hands.

effects.log: You drink without waiting for him. He relaxes. You talk until sunset.

ok.log: He shows you a form and you understand it at once, as if you had always known it.

fail.log: He shows you a form and you understand nothing. He is pleased.

events.text: You visit the court of {pw_kingdom}. The king's chamberlain makes you wait three hours to see whether you will complain.

effects.log: You wait. When you are seen, the king is very gracious.
The chamberlain is surprised. The next day you are seen at once.

events.text: In the hall you are visiting, a child of the household follows you about, asking whether you have ever seen the sea.

effects.log: You describe the sea. The child is so happy that you wonder where you learned to describe it so well.

choices.text: Promise to take them one day.

effects.log: You promise. Ten years later, the child comes to collect.

events.text: Your ally's lord asks you to send soldiers for a quarrel that is not yours. He says the pact demands it. You are not sure it does.

effects.log: You send them. Your ally is grateful. Your own valley is thin that winter.

ok.log: The pact says 'aid', not soldiers. You send grain instead.

fail.log: The pact is clear. You send them, late.

events.text: Your ally wants to seal the pact with a marriage between your families. Two young people who have never met are expected to be pleased.

effects.log: They meet and dislike each other. The pact survives anyway.
The wedding is lavish. The couple are polite to each other for fifty years.

events.text: You learn that your ally has been talking secretly with {hw_foe}. The letter is in his own hand.

effects.log: He apologises and explains. You keep the pact and lock your doors.
You break it at the market cross. It costs you an ally and buys you a name.

events.text: You bring the two sides to the inn at the crossroads. They argue for a day about who sits by the fire.

effects.log: Everyone is cold. Nobody argues about the fire. They argue about the war instead, which is progress.
They take turns by the fire, hourly. It works.

events.text: Each side says the other holds more prisoners than it admits.

ok.log: You walk to every camp and count. Your numbers are trusted.

fail.log: Your numbers are doubted by both.

effects.log: All the prisoners go home. Both sides grumble. Mothers weep at the crossroads.

events.text: Someone keeps spoiling the talks: lost letters, a broken cart, a rumour. You catch a young soldier at it. His brother died at {hw_field}.

effects.log: You talk all night. He does not stop hating, but he stops spoiling.
He is sent home. The talks go faster.

events.text: The treaty is nearly done. One side wants it called a peace. The other wants it called an end to hostilities. Neither will sign the other's word.

effects.log: Both sides sign it. Nobody remembers the words; everybody remembers the inn.
They sign a treaty with no name. It holds.

events.text: Your old company holds a reunion at the inn. There were sixty of you once. Fourteen come.

effects.log: You eat and remember. Someone reads the names of the absent.
You pay. It is more than you can afford and exactly what you wanted.

events.text: You dream of {hw_field} again: the fog, the shouting, the river.

effects.log: You tell your neighbour, another veteran. She has the same dream.
You walk the fields until the sun comes up. The birds help.

events.text: A veteran of {hw_foe} has moved to your village. You fought on the same field, on opposite sides.

effects.log: He comes. You compare scars. By the end you are friends.
You nod. He nods. That is enough for a while.

events.text: Your old staff from the war leans in a corner. A boy of the village asks to borrow it for his first lesson at the school.

effects.log: He takes it to Granny Ahn's school. She recognises it and makes him work twice as hard.
You teach him the first form. He is slow on the left, like you were.

events.text: Old Wol has kept the toll bridge on the river for fifty years. Now both armies want it, and he will not leave. His granddaughter, Dami, a fierce girl who carries his toll box, asks you to make him see sense. Wol, sitting on the rail, says the bridge has outlived three kings and will outlive this war, if people stop asking him to get off it.

choices.text: Stay on the bridge with him.

effects.log: You sit on the rail beside Wol. Dami brings you both rice. The soldiers on both banks find this very awkward.
Wol bites you. Dami apologises for him and does not mean it.

events.text: {hw_cmdr} of {hw_foe} rides up to the far end of the bridge. He is polite. He says the bridge will be burned at dawn, keeper or no keeper. Dami has hidden the toll box. Wol is asleep on the rail with his hat over his face.

ok.log: {hw_cmdr} looks at the sleeping old man for a long time and rides away. The bridge stands.

fail.log: {hw_cmdr} shakes his head and rides back to his lines.

effects.log: Wol pulls the hat down further. 'Then I shall be warm at dawn,' he says.

events.text: Dawn. You are still on the bridge, with Wol and Dami. The soldiers sent to burn it stand on the bank with their torches and do not come. One of them, at last, sits down. Then another. By noon there are forty soldiers of both sides sitting on the riverbank, watching an old man fish off his own bridge.

effects.log: You catch nothing. Wol catches three. The soldiers cheer every fish. Nobody burns anything that day, or the next.
You talk to them. They are farm boys and tired. A few of them go home.

events.text: Years later, Dami is the keeper now. The bridge has a small carved figure of an old man in a hat on its rail. Dami charges you no toll. 'Grandfather left a note,' she says. 'It says: the one who sat with me crosses free. Forever. He underlined forever.'

effects.log: You cross. It is just a bridge. It is the best bridge in the world.
Dami refuses the coin. You leave it on the rail by the carved figure. In the morning it is gone, and a fish is there instead.

events.text: At dawn the bridge burns. Wol and Dami are carried off it by soldiers of both sides, kicking. Wol stands on the bank and watches his bridge go without a word. Dami does not cry. She still has the toll box.

effects.log: You promise. Wol looks at you as if you are very young. 'Then start,' he says.
They stay with you for the winter. Wol fixes everything in your house, badly.

events.text: The war is long over. Dami has rebuilt the bridge, plank by plank, with the toll box money and the help of half the valley. Wol is gone. His hat hangs on the first post. Dami stops you at the toll and grins. 'You owe me,' she says. 'Grandfather said you would come back.'

effects.log: You pay double. Dami puts it in the old box. 'For the next war,' she says. 'To rebuild it again.'

choices.text: Ask to be the keeper's helper for a season.

effects.log: You collect tolls for a season. It is the most peaceful season of your life.

events.text: The Feud of the Schools has gone on for sixty years, and both masters are old now. Granny Ahn of your school and Teacher Ryeo of the other were once students together under the same roof. Each of them has asked you, separately, to deliver a challenge to the other. The challenges are identical, word for word.

effects.log: They each read the other's challenge. Each is outraged by how familiar the wording is.

choices.text: Tell each one the other wrote the same words.

effects.log: Granny Ahn laughs until she has to sit down. Teacher Ryeo, they say, smiled.

events.text: Granny Ahn and Teacher Ryeo meet on the hill between their schools, as their challenges said. Both are carrying staves. Both are carrying a flask of rice wine. They look at each other's flasks for a long time.

effects.log: You walk down the hill. When you look back, they are sitting on a stone, drinking and pointing at the valley.
There is no score to keep. They talk about the teacher they shared. You learn more about your own school in an hour than in years.

events.text: Word comes from both schools on the same morning: the feud is ended, by order of both masters. Students on both sides are furious. Granny Ahn gives you a staff of black wood. 'Teacher Ryeo carved it,' she says. 'He says you are slow on the left.'

effects.log: You become the first student to train under both roofs. Both masters criticise you constantly. It is the happiest you have ever been.

choices.text: Keep the staff on the wall.

effects.log: You hang it on the wall. Students from both schools come to look at it.

events.text: Granny Ahn and Teacher Ryeo fight their duel on the hill. It is very slow, very correct and goes on until sunset. Neither wins. At the end, both are leaning on their staves, out of breath, glaring. Neither will go home first.

effects.log: You carry up two chairs. They sit. They argue about the chairs. Then about the old days.

choices.text: Call it a draw, as judge.

ok.log: Both accept a draw, grudgingly. It is the first draw in sixty years.

fail.log: Both insist they won and go home angry.

events.text: Teacher Ryeo has died in his sleep. Granny Ahn walks to his funeral alone, over the hill, carrying his old challenge, word for word the same as hers. She asks you to read both aloud at the grave.

effects.log: You read both. The students of both schools stand together. The feud does not survive the afternoon.
You read hers. Granny Ahn reads his, herself, in a voice that does not shake once.

events.text: Nabi is the best scout in {hw_side}'s army and nobody believes her, because she is young and quiet and from the reed villages. She brings you a report: {hw_cmdr}'s army is coming by the marsh road, not the hill road. The general is waiting on the hill road.

effects.log: The general hears her out, because you stand beside her. He moves half the army. It is enough.

choices.text: Pass the report on in your own name.

effects.log: The general believes you. Nabi says nothing at all.

events.text: Nabi is made a captain of scouts, the first from the reed villages. Her mother walks three days to see her sworn. Nabi asks you to stand beside her at the swearing, because she is afraid she will forget the words.

effects.log: She does not forget a single word. Her mother cries all through it.
You drill her all night. She says them perfectly, and adds a line of her own about the reeds.

events.text: Years after the war, Nabi sends you a letter from the reed villages. She has started a school for scouts there. 'Nobody here is believed either,' she writes. 'We are going to be so good that they have to.'

effects.log: You send what you can. She names a reed boat after you.

choices.text: Go and teach there for a season.

effects.log: You teach map-reading in a reed hut. The students are terrifying.

events.text: Nabi has been sent back to the reed villages. The general says she was not needed. She left without saying goodbye. On your cot she left a map of the marsh road, very fine, with your name on it as the one who found it.

effects.log: You tell him. He shrugs. You send Nabi a letter and a share of your pay.
You keep it. It is the best map you have ever seen. You never use it without thinking of her.

events.text: Long after the war, a woman in reed sandals stops you at a market. It is Nabi, older, with a basket of eels. She looks at you a long time. 'You kept the map,' she says. It is not a question.

effects.log: You apologise. She listens to all of it. Then she sells you an eel, at full price, and almost smiles.
She takes it, unrolls it and laughs. 'The marsh has moved,' she says. 'It was always going to.'
